function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** that you can follow locally (or in a CI environment) to finish the tasks you listed.  
I’ll also provide the exact file contents that you should add to the repository.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually clone the repo, run `git add`, `commit` or `push` from here, but the instructions below will let you do it yourself.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & create the required artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

The repo contains a simple Node.js app (`app.js`) that listens on port **3000**.  
A minimal, production‑ready Dockerfile looks like this:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install --production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> Save this as `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Using the helper function `create_kubernetes_yaml_file` (the function accepts any image name), we’ll generate a deployment + service that uses the image we’ll build from the Dockerfile.

```yaml
# kubernetes.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry/tag if needed
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 3000
    targetPort: 3000
```

> Save this as `kubernetes.yaml` in the root of the repo.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a workflow that builds the Docker image and pushes it to a registry whenever code is pushed to `main`.  
Place the file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

      - name: Push image to Docker Hub
        run: |
          docker push nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
```

> **Important** – Add the following secrets to your GitHub repo settings:
> * `DOCKER_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub (or other registry) username
> * `DOCKER_PASSWORD` – your Docker Hub password or an access token

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile kubernetes.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

That’s it! After the push, GitHub Actions will automatically run the workflow, build the Docker image, and push it to your registry. The Kubernetes manifests can be applied with `kubectl apply -f kubernetes.yaml` once you’re ready to deploy.
